text:
The Economics Behind the Norman Conquest: Who Actually Got Paid to Invade England?

William the Conqueror didn't have a payroll for Hastings. No invoice for the fleet. No daily wage table for the army. So how did an invasion actually get financed — and who really profited when it succeeded?

This episode follows the money from the Norman coast to the Domesday Book. We trace the Ship List that put 776 vessels into William's fleet, the magnates who bankrolled their own transport and followers, the treasure and tribute that flowed the moment the crown was won, and the tax system William inherited rather than built.

Then we follow one man's ledger from start to finish: Robert of Mortain, credited with the largest single contribution in the Ship List — 120 ships. Twenty years later, Domesday Book shows him holding roughly 797 manors, 248 of them in Cornwall alone. What happened in between — rebellion, castle-building, garrison costs, and the political risk of falling out of favor — is the real story of how conquest turns into wealth.

By 1086, England's royal demesne had nearly doubled in value while the old English landholding elite had been reduced to a fraction of the country's wealth. This is the P&L of 1066: what it cost to invade, what it paid to win, and why the biggest fortunes weren't made in cash.

title: The Economics Behind a Medieval Toll Bridge

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

text:
The economics behind a medieval toll bridge look simple from the outside. One river, one crossing, a gate, and everybody who wants the far bank pays on the way past.

Then you open the accounts.

London Bridge, 1420 to 1421. Rent taken in: fifty pounds and ten shillings. Tolls taken from everyone who crossed: fifteen shillings and two pence. Same bridge, same twelve months — and the gate everybody pictures brought in a fraction of one percent of what the buildings on top of it did.

That gap is where this episode starts. It is not where it ends.

Because the number I actually went looking for does not exist. What did one of these things sell for? What did a man pay to hold one? I searched every English crossing with surviving accounts — London, Rochester, York — expecting a burnt roll or a missing deed. There is no price anywhere, and the reason is not that the records are damaged. It is that the sale they would have recorded could not legally happen.

So this is the system underneath the toll: who really collected it, who really owned the stonework, where the money went, and why an institution that has been earning since the thirteenth century made almost nobody personally rich.

Told through the people whose names are actually in the books. John Woode, who paid twenty pounds a year for the right to collect the cart toll and keep the surplus. The York bridgemasters, whose job title contained the word "bridge" and whose duties did not include the bridge. And two elected wardens a year, every year, walking into a post they could never sell, never inherit, and never keep a penny of.

Real figures from surviving account rolls. Historical currency only, anchored to what a mason earned that same week. Where the record runs out, I say so instead of filling the gap.

📘 The Owner's Ledger — the book behind this channel, on the gap between a business that earns and an owner who keeps: https://theexpensivepart.gumroad.com/...

SOURCES

PRIMARY — Harding & Wright, eds., London Bridge: Selected Accounts and Rentals, 1381–1538, London Record Society 31 (1995) [all London figures: rents, tolls, wages, lead, brick, solder, drawbridge, repast, rent share] · Stell, York Bridgemasters' Accounts, Archaeology of York 2.2 (2003) [44 rolls, 1393 charter, fourpence wain toll] · Catterick Bridge indenture, 1421/22, in Archaeological Journal 7 (1850) · Calendar of Patent Rolls [pontage grants] · TNA Ancient Petitions SC 8/290/14460 (Hastingues/Bayonne), SC 8/220/10962 & SC 8/319/E408 (Corbridge), SC 8/147/7344 (Rochester).

SECONDARY — Cooper, Bridges, Law and Power in Medieval England, 700–1400 (2006) · Harrison, The Bridges of Medieval England (2004) · Gerhold, London Bridge and Its Houses, 1209–1761 (2019) · Haasl, The London Bridge House, c.1209–1554 (2022) · Yates & Gibson, eds., Traffic and Politics: Rochester Bridge, AD 43–1993 (1994) · Trotter, "Bridging the Gap" (2010) · Magnusson, "Urban Infrastructures and Environmental Risk in Medieval England," Environmental Archaeology 28 (2021) · Taylor, "Toll Disputes, Grain Marketing, and Economic Culture in England," Historical Journal 66 (2023) · Roach, "Building Bridges" (2008) · Hohenberg & McCants on social overhead capital (1995) · Thomson, Chronicles of London Bridge (1827) · Stow, A Survey of London (1598).

ARCHIVES — City Bridge Foundation official history [1269 Eleanor of Provence diversion; 1282 and 1319 charters; five bridges funded today] · Rochester Bridge Trust official history [1382 commission incl. Yevele; 1387–91 build; 560 ft, 11 arches, 12 piers, ~10,000 piles; Whittington; 1399 patent].

ON THE NUMBERS — The Catterick sum is contested (250 marks or £173 6s), so the video says "around a hundred and seventy pounds" rather than invent precision. No medieval English bridge leaves a traffic count, so no daily footfall is given. No annual profit margin is calculable from these rolls, and the video says so instead of building one.

An inn didn't make its money on the bed — a night's lodging was some of the cheapest ink in the account book. We went through the surviving accounts for one real inn on the road to London — built by a college that spent eleven years and four hundred pounds on it before collecting a single shilling of rent — to work out who actually got rich running places like this, and who just inherited someone else's debt.

text:
Four people stopped at the same counter in Venice on one afternoon. Only one of them was sick.

A woman spent most of a month's household money on a folded paper packet she couldn't read. A painter's boy came in for blue — a colour that cost more by weight than gold. A steward in good livery bought a great deal and paid for none of it. A fourth man said he had rats. He didn't have rats.

The sick woman was the least profitable person to walk through that door all day.

This is the shop that sold spice, sugar, and the pigment behind Renaissance altarpieces out of the same jars as its medicine — plus a plague-era perfume aristocrats wore against bad air, plus, quietly, an ounce of ground human remains, stocked for decades as a legitimate cure. Grinding made every one of those jars unreadable, and unreadable is exactly what the business was built on. A law from a 13th-century Sicilian king made sure the customer had nowhere else to take that risk but you.

Then it turned around and ate its own trade from the inside, and the sharpest legal case survives from a man who genuinely did not have rats.

Could you actually get rich running one? Only if medicine was never the real business.

Nine things you need to build a medieval ship. Not one of them survives the contract — and the ship itself was never yours.

In 1294, Edward I ordered war galleys from twenty English ports at once. Because the money was never in building. Venice's Arsenal, the most famous shipyard in Europe, spent its first two hundred years as a repair shop. Then in 1468, on the River Usk, a cradle gave way under a ship mid-refit — and took the yard's entire season down with it.

Four grown men are sleeping on the floor three feet from your bed. Your dinner went cold forty-five minutes ago because three servants had to lick your gravy first to make sure it wouldn't stop your heart. And despite owning an entire country, you just had to pawn your crown to a German merchant to pay rent.

Most people think being a medieval king meant sitting on a velvet throne, eating roasted meat, and swimming in gold coins. That’s a children’s book. In this video, we break down what it was actually like to be a king in the Middle Ages—using surviving royal household rolls, kitchen ledgers, and court chronicles from 12th- to 14th-century England and France.

From touching the oozing neck sores of 1,736 peasants a year to prove God chose you, to packing your bed onto a mud-splattered cart 14 times a month because 500 courtiers destroyed the castle plumbing, medieval kingship wasn't freedom. It was a hostage situation with a dress code.

What did it actually cost to own a medieval stained-glass workshop—and could you get rich doing it?

In 1408, John Thornton was paid £56 to create York Minster’s enormous Great East Window. Six centuries later, conserving that same window cost £11.5 million and 92,400 hours of work.

But the real economics of medieval stained glass weren’t in the finished windows.

They were in imported glass, skilled labour, seven-year apprenticeships, maintenance contracts, dangerous workshops, fragile supply chains—and, most importantly, the drawings that could be reused again and again.

In this episode of The Historical Ledger, we open the books on a medieval stained-glass workshop and follow the money from the first sheet of glass to the final commission.

We look at:

• Why English glaziers depended on expensive imported coloured glass
• What medieval glass-painters, glaziers and designers were actually paid
• How workshops survived war, plague and unreliable patrons
• Why cathedral commissions were often less important than repair work
• How reusable “scrolls” of designs became a workshop’s most valuable asset
• The business trick behind medieval flashed ruby glass
• How some glaziers climbed from craftsmen to wealthy civic leaders
• And why the Reformation destroyed not just the windows—but the business model itself

The surprising lesson is that a stained-glass workshop was never really in the business of making windows.

The glass was the invoice. The scroll was the estate.

title: The Economics of Owning a Medieval Manor
channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

aboutChannelInfo.channelDescription: Subscribe to discover the real costs, hidden risks, and surprising economics behind owning essential local businesses.

text:
Could you actually get rich owning a medieval manor?

One year of this business survives in full. The account for Cuxham in Oxfordshire runs from 26 July 1316 to 25 July 1317, written up by a clerk who was paid two shillings for the job—and two more for doing it well. Every penny in, every penny out, on an estate of under five hundred acres.

Read the wheat prices and something is wrong. Grain leaving this manor sold at fourteen and sixteen shillings a quarter. Three years earlier, a quarter of wheat went for about five. That gap is the Great Famine—which means the best-documented cash year in this manor’s history was the year the country was starving.

The costs are stranger. Every permanent worker on the estate—two hostlers, two drivers, a carter, a shepherd, a cowherd, a dairyman, and the clerk who wrote the account—came to sixteen shillings for the whole year. Less than the hay bill. Less than one draught horse.

So where was the money?

Not in the wheat, which barely covered the year. It was in the lines that had almost nothing to do with farming: mill tolls, court fees, inheritance payments, and death duties.

Adam atte Hethe died during this accounting year. His copper pot was carried out of his house and sold for two shillings, and the man who took his land paid forty. One tenant dying was worth nearly three times what the entire permanent staff cost for twelve months.

And the manor’s biggest labour supply never appears in the accounts at all—which is exactly why 1349 destroyed the model.

📘 The Owner’s Ledger: 10 Dead Businesses. 10 Rules That Survived.

If this kind of historical reconstruction is why you watch the channel, I built a complete illustrated field guide from ten surviving businesses across fifteen centuries. It reveals the rules of cash, income, trust, production, and risk that kept appearing long before modern business books existed.

Each rule includes the surviving evidence, the number that decided the outcome, its modern application, and where the rule breaks.

Read it as history. Use it as a business diagnostic.
